threads.body: The comment says “Use the last segment of the file path as the database name”, but the implementation sets the full `filePath` (which can include directories, e.g. `/tmp/mydb`). To match the behavior used in the `resource:` and `file` branches (and the stated intent), extract the last path segment (after the final `/`) before calling `ctx.databaseName(...)`.

For JDBC URLs like `jdbc:sqlite:file:mydb` (file-backed DB without a slash in the path), `sqliteUrl` is `file:mydb`, so the `else` branch sets `databaseName` to `file:mydb` (including the `file:` prefix). Consider handling `sqliteUrl.startsWith("file:")` for the file subtype as well (not only the `mode=memory` case) and strip the `file:` prefix before deriving the last segment.

Returning early makes the parameterized test case pass rather than show as “skipped”, which can hide coverage gaps and is harder to interpret in CI reports. Prefer using a JUnit assumption (e.g., `Assumptions.assumeFalse("sqlite".equals(system), "...")`) so the SQLite variant is reported as skipped.

This is brittle in two ways: (1) it assumes exactly two extra spans will be emitted during SQLiteDataSource initialization, and (2) it detects “javaagent” mode via a class-name substring check. If the number/order of PRAGMA-related spans changes across sqlite-jdbc versions or configuration, this can become flaky. Consider switching to a more robust assertion strategy (e.g., assert the required spans and allow additional spans), and use a more explicit signal for javaagent vs library mode if one exists in this test base.

threads.body: `jdbcUrl` is expected to be a full JDBC URL in this parsing layer (e.g., tests provide values like `jdbc:sqlite:...`). Substringing from `"sqlite:".length()` will cut the string at the wrong position and break parsing (e.g., `"jdbc:sqlite:memory:"` becomes `"lite:memory:"`). Parse should strip the `"jdbc:sqlite:"` prefix (or locate the `"sqlite:"` segment after `"jdbc:"`) before extracting the SQLite-specific portion.

threads.body: `trace.anySatisfy(...)` in this test suite is designed to provide a `SpanDataAssert`-style assertion object to the consumer (as used elsewhere in this same method via `span1 -> span1.hasName(...)`). Wrapping `span` with `org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat(span)` changes the asserted type and will not provide `hasName(...)` / `hasKind(...)` methods, causing compilation failures or incorrect assertions. Use the provided `span` assertion object directly (consistent with the `else` branch), rather than re-wrapping it with AssertJ’s generic `assertThat`.
